card.hook: Look for the building with ship masts sticking out of its roof. That's not a joke: they're stylised masts that show how tall the Vasa stood when fully rigged, and they make the museum very easy to spot.
card.stand_here: Face north-west and you'll see the roofline with boats moored in the harbour in front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole roofline with the boats in front. If you're close and the roof and masts won't fit, try zoom 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the masts and roof detail.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the roofline along the upper third and the moored boats along the bottom, and keep your phone level so the masts stand straight.
card.best_time: Softer morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the copper roof and the water. Midday sun can cause glare off the harbour.
card.selfie_here: Head to the top floor of the Vasa Museum and look for the spot the museum has marked with a selfie sticker. Use the front camera and tilt it so the ship fills the background behind your shoulder. It's worth confirming the marker is still there when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the path along the water outside the museum while you stand in front of the building, so they can fit the whole museum in behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks are not allowed inside the museum, so keep your arm out for the top-floor selfie. Check the official site for photo rules and ticket details before you go.
card.challenge: Can you get the masts on the roof and at least one of the four museum ships in the harbour in the same shot, with nobody's head in the way?
card.good_to_know: The 64-gun warship Vasa sank on her maiden voyage in 1628. She's the only almost fully intact 17th-century ship ever salvaged. The museum opened on 15 June 1990, and you can see the ship from six levels inside.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Galärparken, about 45 m south-east of the museum, on the waterfront edge where the phone icon is. Face north-west and you'll see the roofline with boats moored in the harbour in front.

card.hook: Stortorget is called the Grand Square, but it never tried to be grand. The buildings around it were added bit by bit and a little haphazardly, which gives it an uneven, lived-in look that photographs really well.
card.stand_here: Head for Stortorget, in the middle of Gamla Stan. Stand about 10 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole width of the square and its façades in one frame. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the gables and the cupola.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line up the edges of the buildings with the vertical lines, and keep a strip of cobbles at the bottom of the frame so people can feel how big the space is.
card.best_time: If you like it busy and full of colour, the square is known for its Christmas market. In the evening or at the market, try night mode and hold your phone steady against your body or a wall.
card.selfie_here: Climb the steps of the old Stock Exchange (now the Nobel Prize Museum) so the colourful façades fill the frame behind you. Or stand beside the old well in the middle of the square for a wide shot with the façades and cafés. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the buildings over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand at the south end of the square, facing north toward the Nobel Museum, while you stand in the square with the row of coloured façades behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Stortorget is a public square, but the Nobel Museum and other buildings around it may have their own opening rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find number 3, the blue house with cloverleaf-shaped gables, and get it in one shot with a bit of cobbled ground at the bottom.
card.good_to_know: Stortorget is the oldest square in Stockholm and the historic heart of Gamla Stan. The Stock Exchange Building on the north side was designed by Erik Palmstedt and built between 1773 and 1776, and today it houses the Swedish Academy and the Nobel Museum. Number 3 (Grillska huset) got its cloverleaf gables in 1718. Right next to it: Stockholm Cathedral (Storkyrkan). Right next to it: German Church.

card.good_to_know: The museum opened in May 2013 and is the permanent home of the ABBAWORLD exhibition, which toured Europe and Australia in 2009–2011. card.hook: Djurgården changes its mind every few steps: boats and water in one shot, tall trees and old wooden buildings in the next. Don't plant yourself in one spot, because this island rewards walkers.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 1.4 km north-west of the subject, and face south-east to take in Djurgården's shoreline and buildings. Once you're on the island, walk along the waterfront, because every stretch looks different.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the big scene. From the phone icon, try 2x to pull the shoreline and buildings closer, and keep a bit of foreground in the shot for depth. On the island, go back to 1x for paths, gates and shopfronts, or 0.5x for close waterfront and park views.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on the top or bottom line, then tap the brightest part of the sky or water and slide it a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and fewer people. In midday sun, duck under the trees for shade.
card.selfie_here: Try the southern end of Djurgårdsbron (Djurgården Bridge), where the Blue Gate comes into view after you cross. Use the front camera at 0.5x and turn so the gate sits over your shoulder. It's the likeliest spot, so check the gate fits in the frame before you tap.
card.rules_and_safety: Djurgården's parks and paths are open, but each museum, attraction and the Blue Gate café has its own rules, so check their official sites before you go.
card.challenge: Get three photos in ten minutes: one with water, one with tall trees, one with an old building. Then pick your favourite and call it the island's best angle.
card.good_to_know: Djurgården was once a royal game park. Its name comes from King John III's 1579 plan to keep deer, reindeer and elk there. Gröna Lund opened in 1883 and Skansen in 1891, and many buildings in the west date from the 1897 Stockholm World's Fair.

card.hook: Picture this: you walk past a 16th-century farmhouse, then a lane with someone in 19th-century dress, and a moose is somewhere up the hill. All of that fits in one afternoon, and your camera roll will thank you.

card.zoom: Start at 1x for buildings and village scenes. Go to 0.5x in tight lanes or open squares, and use 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for animals and craft details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put a path or fence line on one of the lower lines, so it leads the eye straight to a building.
card.best_time: Early or late in the day gives softer light on the timber buildings and fewer people in your shots. In early December the Christmas market is busy, so keep your phone ready for the evening lights.
card.selfie_here: Head to Bollnäs Square and stand in front of the wooden handicraft stalls for a close selfie with a historic backdrop. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the stalls sit over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Skansen is a working museum and zoo, so stay on the paths and keep out of other visitors' way while you line up a shot. It's likely ticketed with set opening times, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a path that leads to a building, line it up on the gridlines, then wait for someone in period dress to wander into the frame.
card.good_to_know: Skansen is Sweden's oldest open-air museum, opened by Artur Hazelius on 11 October 1891. He bought around 150 houses from across the country and had them rebuilt here, including the Skogaholm Manor house of 1680. The Christmas market on Bollnäs square has run since 1903.

card.hook: Picture a still morning on the Stockholm waterfront, where the Grand Hôtel shows up twice: once on the shore and once upside down in the water. It's one of those easy wins where the scenery does the work.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x, with the hotel in the middle third and some water in front. Want the quayside, boats and hotel all in one? For the facade, flags or windows, try zoom 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) instead of walking closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the building upright, then tap the hotel front and slide a little darker if the sky is bright so the building keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Early morning or the hour before sunset usually gives soft light and calmer water. In the evening the lights come on and the reflections look great in night mode, so rest your elbows on a railing or wall to keep your phone steady.

card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the Strömkajen promenade to shoot back toward the Grand Hôtel along the waterfront, with you standing between them and the hotel.

card.good_to_know: On a still day the water doubles the hotel in reflection. Passing boats add movement and scale without any effort from you. The Grand Hôtel sits about 167 m south-east of the stand-here point, so you can walk closer if you want.

card.hook: Nearly eight million red bricks sounds heavy, but City Hall sits right on the water and looks surprisingly graceful. Your job is to catch that dark red against the open blue.
card.stand_here: Stand about 25 m north-east of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, near the water on the eastern tip of Kungsholmen. Face south-west and shoot the walls, turrets and details.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x and tilt up for dramatic shots of the brick walls and tower. Use 1x for balanced views, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out turrets, golden starlets, balconies and statues.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line up the walls and tower with the vertical lines, which is easiest if you stand square to the wall.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to red brick than harsh midday sun. Dusk works too: switch on night mode and rest your phone on a wall or railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Head to the courtyard in Stadshusparken by the water, at the foot of the building. Face the water toward Gamla Stan so City Hall is behind you, use the front camera and try 0.5x to squeeze more of the building over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For the whole building in one shot, stand on Evert Taubes Terrass on the western shore of Riddarholmen, with City Hall across the water, and ask someone to take your photo there.
card.rules_and_safety: The building and tower are a major attraction and may have access restrictions or ticketed entry, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Zoom in to 5x (or the most your phone offers) and find the golden starlets on a turret, then see if you can get them in a shot with the Three Crowns on top of the tower.
card.good_to_know: Stockholm City Hall (Stadshuset) is where the Nobel Prize banquet is held. It was built between 1911 and 1923 using nearly eight million bricks. The tower is 106 metres high and topped with the Three Crowns, the Swedish national symbol.

card.hook: Stockholm has plenty of shiny glass boxes, and then there's this solid old customs house standing among them like it never got the memo. That strong, characterful outline is exactly why it's worth a photo stop.

card.best_time: Soft daylight or the hour around dusk suits a building like this. In the evening, switch on night mode and tuck your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.

card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole building, then find one window or entrance detail and see if you can make it look like a different photo.
card.good_to_know: Fotografiska is a photography museum in a former customs house, built in 1906 in the Art Nouveau style. It was designed by Ferdinand Boberg and is listed as a building of cultural interest. The museum opened here in 2010 and drew more than 500,000 visitors a year as of 2020.

card.hook: The palace has 1,430 rooms, and you'll see exactly none of them. Don't sulk, because the outside is the star here: long, tidy and almost suspiciously symmetrical.
card.stand_here: Stand about 60 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, in the northern part of Gamla stan beside the Norrström. Face south-west and the Royal Palace is right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x. If the building won't fit, tap 0.5x. Then try 2x or more and fill the frame with the rows of windows and stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the roof edge up with a horizontal grid line, and keep your phone level so the long lines stay straight.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows on the stonework than midday. The pale walls also stand out nicely against the sky.
card.selfie_here: Head to the gilded crown on the railing of Skeppsholmsbron (the Skeppsholmen bridge), where people line up the palace behind them. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the palace over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: If you're with a friend, ask someone on the Blasieholmen waterfront to shoot south across the Norrström, so the whole palace and Gamla stan fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the outside from the surrounding public areas. Inside, photos for personal use are generally allowed, usually without flash, but some rooms or exhibitions may restrict it, so check signage.
card.challenge: Fill the whole frame with windows and stonework, then see if your friends can guess it's a palace and not an extremely fancy office block.
card.good_to_know: This is the official residence of the Swedish monarch, and the King uses it for representative purposes as head of state. Nicodemus Tessin the Younger designed the Baroque building to replace the medieval Tre Kronor castle, which burned down on 7 May 1697. Building paused in 1709 because of the Great Northern War, restarted in 1727, and the palace was ready to live in by 1754. A long façade renovation has been going on since 2011, so you may spot some scaffolding or covered sections.

card.hook: Five hundred-ish years ago this was the king's cabbage patch. In late April, locals' beloved Kungsan wears a pink blossom tunnel instead, and yes, it's as pretty as it sounds.
card.stand_here: In Kungsträdgården, stand about 70 m north of the numbered pin and face south. You'll look up the avenue toward the middle of the park.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x and tilt your phone up so the branches arch over the top of the frame. Want more canopy and path in one shot? Try zoom 0.5x. For a tighter shot of blossom against the sky, zoom 2x does the job.
card.make_it_pop: Tap on the blossom, then drag the brightness down a little so the sky doesn't wash out the pink.
card.best_time: Late April is usually when the blossom is out, and early morning beats the crowds. The bloom changes with the spring weather, so timing shifts from year to year.
card.selfie_here: Stand under the pink canopy on the cherry blossom avenue with the park's trees behind you (spring only). Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and hold the phone a little high so the blossom fills the top of the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an open public park, but events can change what's on show, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Can you keep the avenue perfectly symmetrical with branches arching over the top? Turn on gridlines and give it three tries.
card.good_to_know: Locals call the park Kungsan. It was first recorded in 1430 as the king's cabbage garden and later became a royal pleasure garden. The tree-lined avenues arrived in the 1860s, and in 2004, 285 new linden trees were planted.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for City Hall across the water. Switch to 0.5x on the far side of the path to fit the cobbled lane, the houses and the view in one frame. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the City Hall tower or Gamla Stan's spires.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the cobbles or the row of houses along the lower third and keep City Hall in the upper part, with the water line level.
card.best_time: There's no set best time here. In winter, skip icy mornings, because the path isn't salted and the boardwalk sections can get slippery.
card.selfie_here: Take it at the Mariaberget observation deck, which guides call the main photo stop on the path (and where plenty of visitors take selfies). Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold your phone so City Hall sits over your shoulder. For a clearer shot, one guide says the western section near the Mariatorget end is usually less busy.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay behind the edge while you take photos, and keep your phone strap or wrist loop on. A metal safety rail separates you from the drop. In cold weather, wear shoes with grip. One guide says the approaches via Klevgränd are darker and steeper at night.
card.challenge: Get the cobbles, a row of houses and the City Hall tower all in one frame, with the horizon dead level. Bonus points if you're not wobbling to do it!
card.good_to_know: Monteliusvägen is an open public walking path with no entry charge. From along the path you can see Gamla Stan's rooftops and spires and Riddarholmen, with the City Hall tower off to one side. card.hook: Slussen is a building site with a view, so don't be shocked if a crane photobombs your skyline. Work on the big rebuild is still going, and the new bridges and water give you plenty to frame anyway.
card.stand_here: Stand about 60 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. Slussen and Gamla Stan should be straight ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole scene. Go to 0.5x for more bridge and sky, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out rooftops across the water.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on the upper or lower line, and use a railing or the paving as a foreground.
card.best_time: Early morning or around sunset usually gives softer light. After dark, the lit-up bridges and water can look great in night mode.
card.selfie_here: Try the top platform of Katarinahissen (the Katarina Elevator), about 38 m above Slussen, with the Old Town behind you. Fjällgatan, a short walk from Slussen's metro station, is another open spot with wide views toward Gamla Stan. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the landmark over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: At Vattentorget, the square at Slussen, ask a passer-by to take your photo with Gamla Stan and the German Church in the background.
card.rules_and_safety: Slussen is an open public area, but the rebuild may close or change some routes, so check the official site before you go and follow signs and temporary walkways. Check that the Katarina lift is open too.
card.challenge: Get the horizon on a gridline, a railing in front, and the Golden Bridge in the shot, then see if you can do it without a single person walking through.
card.good_to_know: The first lock here dates from 1642, and the 1935 lock was the last major one before the current rebuild. The Golden Bridge (Guldbron), officially Slussbron, opened on 26 October 2020. Work began in 2016 and is scheduled to finish in 2027.

card.hook: This castle-looking building on Djurgården is only about a third of the size its architect planned, and it's still huge. The best way to fit all of it in one shot is from across the water.
card.stand_here: Stand on Djurgårdsbron, about 150 m north of the museum, and face south across the water to the palace-style facade. Keep your phone level and let the building fill the middle of the picture.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to catch the whole facade with the water in front. Then tap 2x for the towers and roofline. Save 0.5x for the other viewpoints, where you'll be closer and want more sky and water.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the building's upright edges up with them, and keep a band of water along the bottom of the frame.
card.best_time: Late morning to early afternoon the sun is in front of you, so the facade can look backlit. A cloudy day gives softer, more even light. A clear, calm day gives the best reflections in the water. For the entrance selfie below, one guide recommends the morning, when the light is soft.
card.selfie_here: Climb the front steps of the main entrance on the Djurgårdsvägen side and stand between the two stone obelisks with the building behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a bit low and tilt up so the entrance fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the bridge abutment on the Strandvägen end of Djurgårdsbron, facing the museum, while you stand a few steps in front of them on the bridge with the building behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge is a public place. If you're going inside the museum, check the official site and its current photography policy first.
card.challenge: Take three frames in a row and see if you can get a clean one with no passer-by or vehicle crossing the foreground. Bonus points if the vertical edges sit perfectly on the grid.
card.good_to_know: The Nordic Museum tells the everyday cultural history of Sweden from 1520 to today. Artur Hazelius, who also founded Skansen, started the collection in the 1870s. Isak Gustaf Clason designed the building, which took 19 years to finish in 1907. Inside, a main hall 126 metres long is dominated by a giant sculpture of King Gustav Vasa.

card.hook: You're standing between a palace and an old square, looking up at a wall far too big for your screen. Don't fight it: this church is better in tall, angled shots and little details than in one wide view.

card.rules_and_safety: This is a working church, so check the official site for visiting times, entry rules and whether photos inside are allowed. If you shoot in the alley at the corner of Stora Gråmunkegränd and Stora Nygatan, watch for pedestrians and cyclists.
card.challenge: Find the lines in the pavement by the east wall that mark where an older choir once stood, and use them to lead the eye up to the church.
card.good_to_know: Storkyrkan is the oldest church in Stockholm and was dedicated in 1306. Inside it keeps much of its late medieval character, but the outside looks Baroque after big changes in the 18th century. It was used for coronations for centuries, and Crown Princess Victoria married there in 2010.

card.hook: You can spot Riddarholmen Church's slim iron spire from across the water long before you reach it, like a sharp pencil poking out of the island. Go and find the spot where it hangs over the bay.
card.stand_here: Stand on Evert Taubes terrass, about 130 m west of the subject, and face east. You'll have the bay in front of you, City Hall and the Söder heights across the water, and the spire rising on the island.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the bay, City Hall and the sky all in one go. Then try 1x for a cleaner view, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the spire or City Hall on its own.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the water along the lower third, then tap the sky and slide it a touch darker so the sunset colours don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go at sunset, when guides say the view across the bay is at its best. If the light fades, try night mode and rest your phone on the terrace railing or a wall to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Try Schering Rosenhanes gränd, the slightly raised cobbled lane on Riddarholmen. Use the front camera at 0.5x, with the winding path and the church behind your shoulder. It's an idea based on views toward the church, so check the angle on site.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the northern part of the island while you stand in the open area in front of the church, so they can fit in the whole church and the pink Stenbock palaces.
card.rules_and_safety: At the church, private photos are fine without flash or selfie sticks, as long as you don't disturb other visitors or tours. Drones aren't allowed. The inside is closed in the cooler months, so check the official site if you hope to go in.
card.challenge: Take the spire three ways: far away from the terrace, framed by cobblestones in the lane, and full-front from Birger Jarls torg. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: Parts of the church date back to the late 13th century, when it was a Franciscan friary. Today it's used only for burials and commemorations, and most Swedish monarchs are laid to rest here. The slim cast-iron spire replaced an earlier one destroyed by lightning in 1835.

card.hook: Nationalmuseum is the calm one in the neighbourhood: a long, pale limestone front that borrows its colour from the sky. Grey day, blue day, pink evening, it just goes along with it.
card.stand_here: Stand on Blasieholmen at the phone icon on the map, about 60 m north-west of the subject, and face south-east. From here the long front fits in the frame without you tilting your phone steeply upward.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole building. If people or a lack of space stop you stepping back, try 0.5x. Then go to 2x or more (depending on your phone) for windows and stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the walls straight, then tap the building and slide it a touch darker so the pale limestone keeps its detail instead of going white.
card.best_time: Softer light earlier or later in the day is kinder to pale stone than harsh midday sun. An overcast sky gives a more even look, just a bit flatter.
card.selfie_here: Try Skeppsholmsbron, the bridge to Skeppsholmen. Stand in the middle, by one of the gilded crowns on the railing, with the museum at the Blasieholmen end in the view. Use the front camera at 0.5x to fit more in. A guide says the museum appears on the right from mid-bridge, but check the frame on the spot.
card.ask_someone: Skeppsholmskajen, the quay on the Skeppsholmen side of the bridge, looks across the water at the museum's facade, so it's a good place to ask a passer-by to take your photo.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside, you can photograph and film without flash or a selfie stick. The museum asks that it isn't used as a setting for portrait or wedding photography, and professional shoots with the museum as a backdrop are generally not allowed, so keep it a quick, casual snap. If you take selfies in the galleries, watch out for anything fragile.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole building, then find a single window and make it your 'portrait of the day'.
card.good_to_know: The German architect Friedrich August Stüler designed it; he also designed the Neues Museum in Berlin. It took from 1844 to 1866 to build and draws on northern Italian Renaissance architecture. The museum was founded in 1792 as the Royal Museum, and after a renovation it reopened on 13 October 2018. The building is about 127 m across.

card.hook: Picture a staircase that slowly squeezes you as you look up it. The walls lean in, the steps shrink, and by the top there's barely room for two people to squeeze past each other.
card.stand_here: Stand at the foot of the steps at the Västerlånggatan end of Mårten Trotzigs gränd, right on the phone icon. Face up the lane so the steps run straight away from you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x, which fits the steps and both walls in one frame. Try 0.5x if you want more of the height, but stay near the middle of the lane so the walls don't lean in. Skip the zooming in, because it makes the lane look wider than it is.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the middle of the steps on the centre line, then tap the steps partway up and slide a little darker so the bright sky at the top doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, before Västerlånggatan fills up with visitors. It's the quietest time, so you'll have fewer people wandering into your shot.
card.selfie_here: Switch to the front camera and try 0.5x so more of the old walls fit in behind you. Hold the phone a little above eye level and let the walls rise over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an open public lane, but building work can close it for short periods, so check when you arrive. The steps are narrow and not suitable for wheelchairs or pushchairs.
card.challenge: Get one shot with a single person climbing the steps, so everyone can see just how tight the squeeze is.
card.good_to_know: The 37 steps tighten from a comfortable width to just 90 centimetres at the narrowest point. The lane is named after Mårten Trotzig, a merchant born in Wittenberg who came to Stockholm in 1581. It was closed off in the mid-19th century, reopened in 1945, and the city confirmed the present name in 1949.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the foot of the steps at the Västerlånggatan end of Mårten Trotzigs gränd, right on the phone icon. Face up the lane so the steps run straight away from you.

card.hook: Halfway across a Stockholm bridge, two gilded crowns glint at you like they know they're the stars. Give them a moment, then take two pictures: one of the whole bridge, one of a crown.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Skeppsholmen Bridge footpath at the phone icon, right by the Gilded Crowns at the middle of the bridge, and stay on the pathway, out of the roadway. For the whole-bridge shot, face along the bridge so the arches and railings lead the eye.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the bridge and the water around it. Go to 0.5x if you want the full run of arches in one frame, then zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for a close shot of a crown.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the crown, then drag the slider to make it a little darker so the gold doesn't wash out against a bright sky, and turn on the gridlines to keep the bridge straight.
card.best_time: Early or late in the day usually gives softer light on the gold and fewer people on the pathways. For the arches, any clear time works.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the footpath beside the crown on the left railing as you come from the city centre, with Gamla Stan behind you. Visitors rarely photograph this crown, so it's quieter. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the crown over your shoulder. On the walk back from Skeppsholmen, you can also stand at the crown and face Strandvägen across the bay of Nybroviken for a different backdrop of façades and boats.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the quay at the Skeppsholmen end of the bridge, where the five arches under the deck show best, and try a shot of you on the bridge with the arches behind.
card.rules_and_safety: The footpaths are only about two metres wide and shared with cyclists and runners, so step aside before you stop for photos. Check the official site before you go in case of works or closures.
card.challenge: Get one frame of the whole bridge with the railings perfectly level on the gridlines, and one crown shot so clean it looks like a postcard.
card.good_to_know: The bridge is 165 metres long with five arches, and the present one opened in 1861 as the first forged iron bridge built in Sweden, made by Motala Verkstad. There's been a crossing here since the 1630s, when a wooden bridge was built for the navy's move to the island. The current bridge was listed as a historical landmark in 1935.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Skeppsholmen Bridge footpath at the phone icon, right by the Gilded Crowns at the middle of the bridge, and stay on the pathway, out of the roadway. For the whole-bridge shot, face along the bridge so the arches and railings lead the eye.

card.hook: A huge formal palace, and right beside it a staircase that points straight at it. Photo spots don't get much more obliging than that.
card.stand_here: Stand about 20 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, in front of the Royal Palace's east front and the Logårdstrappan. Face north-west and the palace and stairway are right ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the whole scene. If the building won't fit, drop to 0.5x, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for stonework and windows.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line up the building's edges with the vertical lines so the palace stands up straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Go in the morning. The east-facing front should catch the early light.
card.selfie_here: Climb the granite Logårdstrappan steps and stop near the top, so the palace's east front rises behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a little low so the building fits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Private photography is allowed at the Royal Palace, but selfie sticks aren't allowed, even outside the palace. Access around the palace can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole scene, then one close-up of the stonework, and see which one you like more.
card.good_to_know: The Logårdstrappan is the stairway beside the Royal Palace. It connects the Logården garden with the palace's east entrance. The big straight lines of the building and the diagonal of the steps are what make this such a good photo spot.

card.hook: You're deep in the Gamla stan lanes, you look up, and a brick tower pops out above the old rooftops like it's playing peekaboo. That's the German Church, and it's tricky to get in one shot, which is half the fun.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the church, where the phone icon on the map sits, with the tower in front of you. You're close, so you'll catch walls, doorways and details, and you'll tilt your phone up for the tower.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the church in its narrow street. Want the whole spire? Walk back along a lane and try 0.5x, keeping the tower away from the very edge of the frame. For the gargoyles and the gilded saint, try 2x or 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and keep your phone upright, so the tower stands tall instead of leaning in.
card.best_time: Early morning is best, because the lanes are quieter. A clear day gives the spire a clean sky behind it. At dusk the tower looks great against a darker sky, and night mode helps if the lane is dim.
card.selfie_here: Head to the bottom of Tyska brinken and face the church steeple. You and the whole steeple fit in one frame there, but it gets crowded later in the day. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and keep the steeple over your shoulder. One guide is from 2018, so check the spot when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: For a far-away shot, stand on the Monteliusvägen walkway in Södermalm and ask someone to step well back and shoot across the water to Gamla Stan, with the German Church in the distance (you'll look small).
card.rules_and_safety: Photos inside the church are usually allowed, but check the current rules at the door. Flash isn't allowed indoors. Visiting inside depends on the season and services, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find the gilded saint above the northern gate, then a gargoyle on the tower, and get both in one photo set.
card.good_to_know: The tower and copper-covered spire reach 96 metres and were finished in 1878, after a fire destroyed the earlier tower. The church grew out of a medieval guild building belonging to German merchants, hence the name. It got its present two-nave form in 1638-1642.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the church, where the phone icon on the map sits, with the tower in front of you. You're close, so you'll catch walls, doorways and details, and you'll tilt your phone up for the tower.
